claim: C1qA, C1qB, and C1qC are the most abundant soluble defense collagen transcripts in the mouse small intestine and colon.
source: The most abundant soluble defense collagen transcripts in the small intestine and colon were those encoding C1qA, C1qB, and C1qC (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: C1qa, C1qb, and C1qc transcripts are most abundant in CD45+ cells compared to CD45- cells in the mouse small intestine.
source: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-sorted cell suspensions recovered from the small intestines of wild-type C57BL/6 mice revealed that C1qa, C1qb, and C1qc transcripts were most abundant in CD45+ cells, which include all immune cells, as compared to CD45- cells, which encompass epithelial cells and other non-immune cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-sorted cells shown in Figure 1B

claim: C1q transcripts and protein are most abundant in CD45+ cells recovered from the subepithelial compartment compared to the intraepithelial compartment of the small intestine.
source: Furthermore, C1q transcripts and protein were most abundant in CD45+ cells recovered from the subepithelial compartment, which includes both the lamina propria and muscularis, as compared to CD45+ cells recovered from the intraepithelial compartment of the small intestine (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: C1q is expressed by immune cells located in the subepithelial compartment of the intestine and is largely absent from epithelial cells and intraepithelial immune cells.
source: Thus, C1q is expressed by immune cells located in the subepithelial compartment of the intestine and is largely absent from epithelial cells and intraepithelial immune cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from the data presented in Figure 1B, C, and D showing differential expression patterns

claim: Expression of C1q transcripts and protein is highest in CD11b+MHCII+F4/80hi macrophages and mostly absent from non-macrophage immune cells.
source: Expression of C1q transcripts and protein was highest in CD11b+MHCII+F4/80hi macrophages and was mostly absent from non-macrophage immune cells (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 1E-H

claim: C1q is expressed by macrophages in the mouse small intestine.
source: Thus, C1q is expressed by macrophages in the mouse small intestine.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data in Figure 1E-H showing macrophage-specific expression

claim: Antibody-mediated depletion of macrophages leads to a >twofold reduction in the number of macrophages recovered from the small intestine.
source: Antibody injection led to a >twofold reduction in the number of macrophages recovered from the small intestine (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B after anti-CSF1R antibody treatment

claim: Antibody-mediated depletion of macrophages results in a corresponding reduction in small intestinal C1q gene expression.
source: Antibody injection led to a >twofold reduction in the number of macrophages recovered from the small intestine (Figure 2B), and a corresponding reduction in small intestinal C1q gene expression (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C after macrophage depletion

claim: Macrophages are the primary source of intestinal C1q.
source: Antibody injection led to a >twofold reduction in the number of macrophages recovered from the small intestine (Figure 2B), and a corresponding reduction in small intestinal C1q gene expression (Figure 2C), suggesting that macrophages are the primary source of intestinal C1q.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between macrophage depletion and C1q reduction shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice lack C1q expression in intestinal macrophages.
source: These mice, hereafter designated as C1qaΔMϕ mice, lacked C1q expression in intestinal macrophages (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice have markedly lower C1q expression in both the small intestine and colon.
source: Importantly, C1qaΔMϕ mice had markedly lower C1q expression in both the small intestine and colon (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Macrophages are the main source of C1q in the intestine.
source: Importantly, C1qaΔMϕ mice had markedly lower C1q expression in both the small intestine and colon (Figure 2G), indicating that macrophages are the main source of C1q in the intestine.
evidence: Inference drawn from the marked reduction in C1q expression in C1qaΔMϕ mice shown in Figure 2G

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice lack C1q gene expression in the lung, skin, kidney, and liver but not the brain.
source: Unexpectedly, the C1qaΔMϕ mice also lost C1q gene expression in the lung, skin, kidney, and liver (but not the brain), and the C1q protein was undetectable in the serum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: C1q protein is undetectable in the serum of C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Unexpectedly, the C1qaΔMϕ mice also lost C1q gene expression in the lung, skin, kidney, and liver (but not the brain), and the C1q protein was undetectable in the serum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: LysM+ macrophages or macrophage-like cells are the main sources of C1q in most extraintestinal tissues and the bloodstream.
source: These findings indicate that macrophages are the primary source of C1q in the intestine and suggest that LysM+ macrophages or macrophage-like cells are also the main sources of C1q in most extraintestinal tissues and the bloodstream.
evidence: Inference drawn from the loss of C1q in multiple tissues and serum in C1qaΔMϕ mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: C1qa is expressed at similar levels in the small intestines of germ-free and conventionally-raised mice.
source: C1qa was expressed at similar levels in the small intestines of germ-free and conventionally-raised mice (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing germ-free and conventional mice shown in Figure 3A

claim: C1q expression is not induced by the intestinal microbiota.
source: C1qa was expressed at similar levels in the small intestines of germ-free and conventionally-raised mice (Figure 3A), suggesting that C1q expression is not induced by the gut microbiota.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of difference in C1qa expression between germ-free and conventional mice shown in Figure 3A

claim: Reg3g is expressed at a >twofold higher level in conventional as compared to germ-free mice.
source: This contrasted with Reg3g, encoding the antimicrobial protein REG3G (Cash et al., 2006), which was expressed at a > twofold higher level in conventional as compared to germ-free mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing germ-free and conventional mice shown in Figure 3A, with citation to Cash et al., 2006

claim: C1q is not detected in the gut lumen of either conventional or germ-free mice.
source: Additionally, in contrast to REG3G, C1q was not detected in the gut lumen of either conventional or germ-free mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B

claim: C1qa expression is not markedly altered by a 24 hr oral infection with Salmonella Typhimurium.
source: C1qa expression was also not markedly altered by a 24 hr oral infection with the intestinal pathogenic bacterial species Salmonella Typhimurium (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data after S. typhimurium infection shown in Figure 3C

claim: C1q is not induced by the gut microbiota or by a 24 hr infection with S. typhimurium.
source: Although we cannot rule out the induction of C1q by longer-term pathogenic infections, these data indicate that C1q is not induced by the gut microbiota or by a 24 hr infection with S. typhimurium, in contrast to other intestinal antibacterial proteins.
evidence: Inference drawn from data in Figure 3A and 3C showing no induction by microbiota or S. typhimurium

claim: Intestinal microbiota composition is not appreciably altered in C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis of the fecal microbiotas of C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice showed that the microbiota composition was not appreciably altered in the absence of macrophage C1q (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 3D

claim: There are no statistically significant differences in translocation of the microbiota to the mesenteric lymph nodes between C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Analysis of 16S rRNA gene copy number in mesenteric lymph nodes further indicated no statistically significant differences in translocation of the microbiota to the mesenteric lymph nodes (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data of 16S rRNA gene copy numbers shown in Figure 3E

claim: The sensitivity of C1qaΔMϕ mice to DSS is similar to that of their C1qafl/fl littermates.
source: However, the sensitivity of the C1qaΔMϕ mice to DSS was similar to that of their C1qafl/fl littermates as assessed by change in body weight and histopathological analysis (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by body weight and histopathology data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: There is no change in intestinal paracellular permeability in C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: There was also no change in intestinal paracellular permeability in C1qaΔMϕ mice as measured by oral administration of FITC-dextran (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by FITC-dextran permeability assay data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Macrophage C1q does not substantially impact gut microbiota composition or intestinal epithelial barrier function.
source: These results suggest that macrophage C1q does not substantially impact gut microbiota composition or intestinal epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Inference drawn from data in Figure 3D, 3E, 3F, and 3G showing no changes in microbiota, translocation, DSS sensitivity, or permeability

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice clear C. rodentium similarly to their C1qafl/fl littermates.
source: However, C1qaΔMϕ mice cleared C. rodentium similarly to their C1qafl/fl littermates (Figure 3H) and showed similar histopathology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by fecal bacterial burden data shown in Figure 3H and histopathology in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: C1q is dispensable for defense against C. rodentium infection.
source: However, C1qaΔMϕ mice cleared C. rodentium similarly to their C1qafl/fl littermates (Figure 3H) and showed similar histopathology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that C1q is dispensable for defense against C. rodentium infection.
evidence: Inference drawn from the similar clearance and histopathology between C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl mice shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There are no statistically significant differences in cytokine expression between C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Measurement of transcripts encoding secreted immune effectors in the small intestines of C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ littermates revealed no statistically significant differences in cytokine expression (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data of cytokine transcripts shown in Figure 3I

claim: There are no statistically significant differences in the percentages or absolute numbers of various T cell subsets between C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Furthermore, there were no statistically significant differences in the percentages or absolute numbers of various T cell subsets, including Thelper1 (TH1), TH2, TH17, and regulatory T (Treg) cells between C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Total B cell numbers trend lower in C1qaΔMϕ mice, but the difference is not statistically significant.
source: Although total B cell numbers trended lower in C1qaΔMϕ mice, the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: There are no statistically significant differences in the percentages or absolute numbers of total plasma cells, IgA+ plasma cells, myeloid cells, or innate lymphoid cells between C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: There were also no statistically significant differences in the percentages or absolute numbers of total plasma cells (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 4), IgA+ plasma cells (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 4), myeloid cells (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 5), or innate lymphoid cells (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 6) when comparing C1qafl/fl and C1qaΔMϕ mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplements 4, 5, and 6

claim: The absence of macrophage C1q has little impact on intestinal immunity.
source: These results suggest that the absence of macrophage C1q has little impact on intestinal immunity.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of significant differences in immune cell populations and cytokine expression shown in Figure 3I and 3J

claim: C1q does not participate substantially in intestinal immune defense.
source: Altogether, our findings suggest that C1q does not participate substantially in intestinal immune defense and thus might have an intestinal function that is independent of its canonical role in activating the classical complement pathway.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective data in Figure 3 showing no major immune defects in C1qaΔMϕ mice

claim: C1q was localized close to submucosal plexus nerve fibers marked with βIII tubulins (TUBB3) in C1qafl/fl mice.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed that C1q was localized close to submucosal plexus nerve fibers marked with βIII tubulins (TUBB3) in C1qafl/fl mice (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: C1q is absent in C1qaΔMϕ mice despite the presence of similar overall numbers of CD169+ macrophages.
source: C1q was absent in C1qaΔMϕ mice despite the presence of similar overall numbers of CD169+ macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: C1q is expressed by macrophages recovered from the muscularis.
source: Although C1q immunoreactivity in the myenteric plexus was less pronounced, flow cytometry analysis indicated that C1q was expressed by macrophages recovered from the muscularis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: RNAscope analysis of LMMP wholemounts revealed C1qa-expressing macrophages next to HuC/D+ neurons.
source: Supporting this finding, RNAscope analysis of longitudinal muscle-myenteric plexus (LMMP) wholemounts revealed C1qa-expressing macrophages next to HuC/D+ neurons (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 4D

claim: C1qa signals are mostly absent in muscularis macrophages of C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Consistent with other validation data (Figure 2E–G), C1qa signals were mostly absent in muscularis macrophages of C1qaΔMϕ mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from RNAscope data in Figure 4D and validation data in Figure 2E-G

claim: C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages show elevated expression of Arginase 1, CD169, and TREM2.
source: Finally, C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages showed elevated expression of Arginase 1, CD169, and TREM2 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2) (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Arginase 1, CD169, and TREM2 are enriched on macrophages with known neuromodulatory functions.
source: Finally, C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages showed elevated expression of Arginase 1, CD169, and TREM2 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2) (Figure 4E), which are enriched on macrophages with known neuromodulatory functions (Colonna, 2003; Paloneva et al., 2002; Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colonna, 2003; Paloneva et al., 2002; Ural et al., 2020

claim: C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages are located near enteric neurons in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses.
source: Thus, C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages are located near enteric neurons in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses and express proteins that are characteristic of nerve-adjacent macrophages in other tissues.
evidence: Inference drawn from immunofluorescence and RNAscope data in Figure 4B, C, and D showing proximity to neurons

claim: C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages express proteins that are characteristic of nerve-adjacent macrophages in other tissues.
source: Thus, C1q-expressing intestinal macrophages are located near enteric neurons in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses and express proteins that are characteristic of nerve-adjacent macrophages in other tissues.
evidence: Inference drawn from flow cytometry data in Figure 4E showing expression of neuromodulatory markers

claim: There is a similar number of HuC/D+ neurons in C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl mice.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of LMMP wholemounts from the small intestine and colon revealed a similar number of HuC/D+ neurons and a similar density of TUBB3+ neuronal fibers (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: There is a similar density of TUBB3+ neuronal fibers in C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl mice.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of LMMP wholemounts from the small intestine and colon revealed a similar number of HuC/D+ neurons and a similar density of TUBB3+ neuronal fibers (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: There are similar numbers of excitatory (Chat+) and inhibitory (Nos1+) neurons in C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl mice.
source: There were also similar numbers of specific neuronal subsets, including excitatory (Chat+) and inhibitory (Nos1+) neurons (Figure 5C and E)
evidence: Supported by RNAscope and qPCR data shown in Figure 5C and E

claim: There is a similar density of S100B+ enteric glial cells in C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl mice.
source: There were also similar numbers of specific neuronal subsets, including excitatory (Chat+) and inhibitory (Nos1+) neurons (Figure 5C and E), and a similar density of S100B+ enteric glial cells (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and qPCR data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: The anatomical features of the enteric nervous system are not appreciably altered in C1qa∆Mφ mice.
source: Thus, the anatomical features of the enteric nervous system are not appreciably altered in C1qa∆Mφ mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from data in Figure 5A-E showing no changes in neuronal numbers or glial cell density

claim: Of the 22 biological pathways enriched in the LMMP of C1qaΔMϕ mice, 17 are related to neuronal development or function.
source: Of the 22 biological pathways that were enriched in the LMMP of C1qaΔMϕ mice, 17 were related to neuronal development or function, including synapse organization, dendrite development, and neurotransmitter secretion (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 30 differentially expressed genes with known roles in regulating neuronal activity, synaptic transmission, and neuropeptide signaling in C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Our analysis also identified 30 differentially expressed genes with known roles in regulating neuronal activity (e.g. Dusp26), synaptic transmission (e.g. Rasgrf2), and neuropeptide signaling (e.g. Tacr2) (Mao et al., 2017; Schwechter et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B with citations to Mao et al., 2017; Schwechter et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017

claim: There is a statistically significant overlap in the transcriptional changes in the colonic LMMP of C1qaΔMϕ mice and the neural crest cells of TashT mice.
source: A comparative analysis revealed a statistically significant overlap in the transcriptional changes in the colonic LMMP of C1qaΔMϕ mice and the neural crest cells of TashT mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Macrophage C1q impacts enteric nervous system gene expression and function.
source: These results suggested that macrophage C1q impacts enteric nervous system gene expression and function.
evidence: Inference drawn from RNA-seq data in Figure 6A and B showing altered neuronal gene expression in C1qaΔMϕ mice

claim: Transit times are decreased in C1qaΔMϕ mice relative to their C1qafl/fl littermates.
source: C1qaΔMϕ and C1qafl/fl littermates were gavaged with the dye and the time to the first appearance of the dye in the feces was recorded. Transit times were decreased in C1qaΔMϕ mice relative to their C1qafl/fl littermates, indicating accelerated gut motility (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by Carmine Red transit assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Decreased transit times in C1qaΔMϕ mice indicate accelerated gut motility.
source: Transit times were decreased in C1qaΔMϕ mice relative to their C1qafl/fl littermates, indicating accelerated gut motility (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inference drawn from the decreased transit time data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Gut transit time is unchanged in C3-/- mice.
source: By contrast, gut transit time was unchanged in C3-/- mice, suggesting that macrophage C1q impacts gut motility independent of its canonical function in the classical complement pathway (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by Carmine Red transit assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Macrophage C1q impacts gut motility independent of its canonical function in the classical complement pathway.
source: By contrast, gut transit time was unchanged in C3-/- mice, suggesting that macrophage C1q impacts gut motility independent of its canonical function in the classical complement pathway (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of C1qaΔMϕ and C3-/- mice shown in Figure 6C

claim: The length of the small intestine and colon are unaltered in C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: This was not due to a change in the length of either the small intestine or the colon, which were unaltered in the C1qaΔMϕ mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by intestinal length measurements shown in Figure 6D

claim: Accelerated transit is observed in the small intestines of C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: Accelerated transit was also observed in the small intestines of C1qaΔMϕ mice as assessed by rhodamine dye transit assay (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by rhodamine B-dextran transit assay data shown in Figure 6E

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice have accelerated colonic motility when compared to C1qafl/fl littermates.
source: To assess colonic motility, we measured the expulsion time after intrarectal insertion of a glass bead and found that C1qaΔMϕ mice had accelerated colonic motility when compared to C1qafl/fl littermates (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by colonic bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 6F

claim: The absence of macrophage C1q results in defective enteric nervous system function and dysregulated gastrointestinal motility.
source: Our results thus suggest that the absence of macrophage C1q results in defective enteric nervous system function and dysregulated gastrointestinal motility.
evidence: Inference drawn from the accelerated transit data in Figure 6C, E, and F

claim: The colons of C1qaΔMϕ mice have increased total number, frequency, and velocity of CMMC compared to C1qafl/fl littermates.
source: Spatiotemporal mapping revealed that the colons of C1qaΔMϕ mice had increased total number, frequency, and velocity of CMMC as compared to C1qafl/fl littermates (Figure 6G and H; Figure 6—video 1; Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo CMMC analysis data shown in Figure 6G and H

claim: The colons of C1qaΔMϕ mice maintain increased neurogenic peristaltic activity compared to their C1qafl/fl littermates even in the absence of gut-extrinsic signals.
source: This indicated that the colons of C1qaΔMϕ mice maintained increased neurogenic peristaltic activity compared to their C1qafl/fl littermates even in the absence of gut-extrinsic signals.
evidence: Inference drawn from the ex vivo CMMC data shown in Figure 6G and H

claim: The absence of macrophage C1q increases enteric nervous system-dependent peristalsis and accelerates gut transit.
source: Thus, the absence of macrophage C1q increases enteric nervous system-dependent peristalsis and accelerates gut transit.
evidence: Inference drawn from the CMMC and transit data shown in Figure 6

claim: Macrophage C1q regulates gastrointestinal motility.
source: Taken together, our findings reveal that macrophage C1q regulates gastrointestinal motility.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective data in Figure 6 showing altered motility in C1qaΔMϕ mice

claim: Macrophages are the primary source of C1q in the mouse intestine.
source: Here, we have identified a role for C1q in regulating gastrointestinal motility. We discovered that macrophages are the primary source of C1q in the mouse intestine and that macrophage C1q regulates enteric neuronal gene expression and gastrointestinal transit time.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 1 and Figure 2

claim: Macrophage C1q regulates enteric neuronal gene expression.
source: Here, we have identified a role for C1q in regulating gastrointestinal motility. We discovered that macrophages are the primary source of C1q in the mouse intestine and that macrophage C1q regulates enteric neuronal gene expression and gastrointestinal transit time.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 6A and B

claim: Macrophage C1q regulates gastrointestinal transit time.
source: Here, we have identified a role for C1q in regulating gastrointestinal motility. We discovered that macrophages are the primary source of C1q in the mouse intestine and that macrophage C1q regulates enteric neuronal gene expression and gastrointestinal transit time.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 6C-H

claim: Serum C1q is produced by liver dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages.
source: Serum C1q is produced by liver dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages (El-Shamy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to El-Shamy et al., 2018

claim: C1q circulates in the bloodstream where it participates in immune defense against infection by recognizing antibodies bound to invading bacteria.
source: C1q circulates in the bloodstream, where it participates in immune defense against infection by recognizing antibodies bound to invading bacteria. This binding interaction initiates the classical complement pathway, which entails the recruitment and proteolytic processing of other complement components that rupture the bacterial membrane and recruit phagocytic cells (Kishore and Reid, 2000; Noris and Remuzzi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kishore and Reid, 2000; Noris and Remuzzi, 2013

claim: C1q is produced by microglia in the brain where it promotes the pruning of neuronal synapses.
source: C1q is also produced by microglia (brain-resident macrophage-like cells) in the brain where it promotes the pruning of neuronal synapses through an unclear mechanism (Hammond et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2016

claim: C1q deficiency results in heightened synaptic connectivity in the central nervous system which can lead to epilepsy.
source: Consequently, C1q deficiency results in heightened synaptic connectivity in the central nervous system which can lead to epilepsy (Chu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chu et al., 2010

claim: Muscularis macrophages regulate enteric neurons and smooth muscle cells that drive gastrointestinal motility.
source: In contrast, muscularis macrophages that reside in deeper intestinal tissues, such as the muscularis externa (Figure 4A), regulate enteric neurons and smooth muscle cells that drive gastrointestinal motility (De Schepper et al., 2018a; De Schepper et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Schepper et al., 2018a; De Schepper et al., 2018b

claim: C1q has several well-described functions in regulating the development and activity of neurons of the central nervous system.
source: Furthermore, C1q has several well-described functions in regulating the development and activity of neurons of the central nervous system (Hammond et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2016

claim: CSF1R+ macrophages selectively localize to the muscularis of the mouse intestine.
source: Prior work has shown that CSF1R+ macrophages selectively localize to the muscularis of the mouse intestine (Muller et al., 2014; Gabanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muller et al., 2014; Gabanyi et al., 2016

claim: Muscularis macrophages secrete BMP2, which activates enteric neurons that regulate colonic muscle contraction and colonic motility.
source: These macrophages secrete BMP2, which activates enteric neurons that regulate colonic muscle contraction and thus colonic motility (Muller et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller et al., 2014

claim: C. rodentium clearance depends on immunoglobulins and complement component C3.
source: Second, C. rodentium clearance depends on immunoglobulins and complement component C3 (Belzer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belzer et al., 2011

claim: Most humans with C1q deficiency develop systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: Additionally, most humans with C1q deficiency develop systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about C1q deficiency

claim: C1q deficiency is thought to result in increased exposure of self-antigen to the immune system, thereby reducing immune tolerance and causing autoimmune disease.
source: Since C1q can target cellular debris for phagocytosis, it is thought that C1q deficiency results in increased exposure of self-antigen to the immune system, thereby reducing immune tolerance and causing autoimmune disease (Macedo and Isaac, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Macedo and Isaac, 2016

claim: Roughly 42.5% of SLE patients report gastrointestinal symptoms that range from acute abdominal pain to chronic intestinal obstruction.
source: Furthermore, roughly 42.5% of SLE patients report gastrointestinal symptoms that range from acute abdominal pain to chronic intestinal obstruction (Fawzy et al., 2016; Tian and Zhang, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fawzy et al., 2016; Tian and Zhang, 2010

claim: C1q deficiency is strongly correlated with SLE in humans.
source: Given that C1q deficiency is strongly correlated with SLE in humans and alters gut motility in mice, we suggest that C1q could be a therapeutic target for SLE patients that present with chronic constipation or other forms of dysregulated intestinal motility.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about C1q deficiency and SLE

claim: C1q deficiency alters gut motility in mice.
source: Given that C1q deficiency is strongly correlated with SLE in humans and alters gut motility in mice, we suggest that C1q could be a therapeutic target for SLE patients that present with chronic constipation or other forms of dysregulated intestinal motility.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 6

claim: C1q could be a therapeutic target for SLE patients that present with chronic constipation or other forms of dysregulated intestinal motility.
source: Given that C1q deficiency is strongly correlated with SLE in humans and alters gut motility in mice, we suggest that C1q could be a therapeutic target for SLE patients that present with chronic constipation or other forms of dysregulated intestinal motility.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the connection between C1q deficiency, SLE, and gut motility

claim: Macrophages that localize to the lamina propria contribute to immune defense against pathogenic bacteria.
source: For example, macrophages that localize to the tissue located directly underneath the gut epithelium — known as the lamina propria — contribute to immune defense against pathogenic bacteria (Gabanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gabanyi et al., 2016

claim: Muscularis macrophages express genes that are distinct from lamina propria macrophages.
source: These muscularis macrophages express genes that are distinct from lamina propria macrophages (Gabanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gabanyi et al., 2016

claim: Muscularis macrophages directly regulate the activity of smooth muscle cells.
source: They directly regulate the activity of smooth muscle cells (Luo et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2018

claim: Muscularis macrophages secrete soluble factors, such as bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), which interact with the enteric neurons that control smooth muscle activity.
source: and secrete soluble factors, such as bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), which interact with the enteric neurons that control smooth muscle activity (Muller et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller et al., 2014

claim: Muscularis macrophages play a key role in regulating gut motility.
source: Muscularis macrophages thus play a key role in regulating gut motility.
evidence: Inference drawn from the cited functions of muscularis macrophages

claim: Interactions between intestinal macrophages and the enteric nervous system regulate gastrointestinal motility.
source: Interactions between intestinal macrophages and the enteric nervous system regulate gastrointestinal motility, yet we have an incomplete understanding of the molecular mediators of this crosstalk.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Peristaltic movement of the intestine propels food down the length of the gastrointestinal tract to promote nutrient absorption.
source: Peristaltic movement of the intestine propels food down the length of the gastrointestinal tract to promote nutrient absorption.
evidence: Established physiological knowledge

claim: Gastrointestinal motility requires coordination of the activity of smooth muscle cells by enteric neurons.
source: The gastrointestinal motility that underlies peristalsis is a complex process that requires coordination of the activity of smooth muscle cells by enteric neurons (Rao and Gershon, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao and Gershon, 2016

claim: Intestinal macrophages impact gastrointestinal motility by regulating the functions of enteric neurons and facilitating their interactions with smooth muscle cells.
source: Several studies have revealed that intestinal macrophages impact gastrointestinal motility by regulating the functions of enteric neurons and facilitating their interactions with smooth muscle cells (Muller et al., 2014; Matheis et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muller et al., 2014; Matheis et al., 2020

claim: C1q is a member of the defense collagen family that has distinct roles in immune defense and nervous system development and function.
source: C1q is a member of the defense collagen family that has distinct roles in immune defense and nervous system development and function (Bossi et al., 2014; Casals et al., 2019; Shah et al., 2015; Thielens et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bossi et al., 2014; Casals et al., 2019; Shah et al., 2015; Thielens et al., 2017

claim: C1q is composed of six molecules each of C1qA, C1qB, and C1qC, forming a 410 kDa oligomer.
source: It is composed of six molecules each of C1qA, C1qB, and C1qC, forming a 410 kDa oligomer.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about C1q

claim: Human macrophages recovered from the intestinal muscularis selectively express C1q when compared to lamina propria macrophages.
source: Indeed, single-cell RNAseq analysis shows that macrophages recovered from the human intestinal muscularis selectively express C1q when compared to lamina propria macrophages (Domanska et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domanska et al., 2022

claim: Dysregulated peristalsis is a characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome.
source: Dysregulated peristalsis is a characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome (Vrees et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vrees et al., 2002

claim: Dysregulated peristalsis is present in a subset of inflammatory bowel disease patients.
source: and is present in a subset of inflammatory bowel disease patients (Bassotti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bassotti et al., 2014

claim: C1qaΔMϕ mice had alterations in at least three highly represented macrophage clusters.
source: We identified 11 unique macrophage clusters and found that C1qaΔMϕ mice had alterations in at least three highly represented clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Analysis of differentially expressed genes across all macrophage clusters indicated lowered representation of transcripts linked to control of macrophage differentiation or functional states in C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: However, analysis of the differentially expressed genes across all macrophage clusters indicated lowered representation of transcripts that are linked to control of macrophage differentiation or functional states, such as Malat1, Neat1, and Etv3 (Cui et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Villar et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D with citations to Cui et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Villar et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019

claim: In macrophages from C1qafl/fl mice, eight 'microglia-specific genes' were expressed whose expression was lowered or lost in macrophages from C1qaΔMϕ mice.
source: In macrophages from C1qafl/fl mice, we observed the expression of eight 'microglia-specific genes' whose expression was lowered or lost in macrophages from C1qaΔMϕ mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Mouse enteric neurons express Adgrb1, which encodes BAI1, a recently identified C1q receptor on human neural stem cells.
source: In support of this idea, we observed that mouse enteric neurons express Adgrb1, which encodes BAI1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), a recently identified C1q receptor on human neural stem cells (Benavente et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and citation to Benavente et al., 2020
